solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Not for the first time, lose confidence in fortification

parts.note: re- means again, so not for the first time
to doubt is to lose confidence in something

explanation.surface: A defender, after one setback too many, starts to lose faith in the walls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose confidence in' reads as one phrase, but the 'in' is only the link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A redoubt is a small, often temporary fortification.

clue.text: Bank calling in a loan upfront? That surprises me

indicators.note: only the front letter of 'loan' is used

parts.note: to bank on something is to rely on it

indicators.note: the bank calls in, i.e. takes in, the other letters

parts.note: kept as is
first letter of loan

explanation.surface: Someone is startled that their bank wants a loan repaid in advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks like a noun, the lender; it is the verb, as in 'bank on', which gives RELY.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Really?' is an exclamation of surprise.

clue.text: Casually stops by with request for repentance

definitions.meaning: the everyday phrasal verb for paying an informal, unplanned visit
a preacher's two-word plea to give up wrongdoing, split after the fourth letter

explanation.surface: A preacher pops round unannounced to urge someone to mend their ways.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase differently: DROP SIN, an instruction a preacher might give.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who drops in makes a casual, unplanned visit.

clue.text: Weaken effect of ceremonial trim after short reverse

indicators.note: the trim comes after the other piece
short = cut off at the end, so UNDO loses its O

parts.note: to reverse a change is to undo it; UNDO without its last letter
ermine fur trims ceremonial robes

explanation.surface: An official's ceremonial outfit loses its impact after a botched backwards step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverse' is a verb here, meaning to undo, not a backward movement.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: literally digging beneath a wall to bring it down, and figuratively sapping the force of an argument or plan.

clue.text: In the first place, I tighten bow that's loose

indicators.note: the letters are loose, free to be rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: An archer, or someone tying a ribbon, first tightens a bow that has come loose.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the front, so 'In the first place' only looks like part of the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: 'To begin with' and 'in the first place' both mean firstly.

clue.text: American choirboy nearly rejected by a province

indicators.note: the last letter is dropped from TREBLE
by = next to, so the final A sits alongside

parts.note: A = American
a treble is a boy soprano; TREBLE without its last letter
kept as is

explanation.surface: A US choirboy nearly gets turned away by a provincial choir.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing 'a' is wordplay, not part of the definition: 'a province' only reads like one.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this western Canadian region, capital Edmonton, is one of the country's ten provinces.

clue.text: Dismiss formal test looking up missing marks

indicators.note: in a down clue, looking up means read from the bottom, so reversed

parts.note: an exam is a formal test; reversed it reads MAXE
M = marks, the old German currency; removed

explanation.surface: A candidate is failed for a formal test that turned up missing marks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks' reads as exam scores, but it is the abbreviation M for the Deutschmark.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal, headline-writer's synonym: firms are said to chop staff, cutting them as a woodsman fells trees.

clue.text: Back in the old days, investment not complicated

indicators.note: the investment is written backwards
in places one thing within another

parts.note: BC, before Christ, stands for ancient times
ISA, an Individual Savings Account, reversed

explanation.surface: Someone recalls that investing used to be simple back in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: An ISA is a British tax-free savings account. 'Back in the old days' reads as one phrase, but splits into two instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something reduced to its essentials, with no frills, is free of complication.

clue.text: Run iron over top half of mac? Don't!

indicators.note: only the first half of RAINCOAT is used

parts.note: R = run, as in cricket scores
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron, reversed
a mac is a raincoat; its first half is RAIN

explanation.surface: A warning not to press a hot iron on a waterproof mac.
explanation.walkthrough: A mac is a raincoat, short for mackintosh. The definition is the exclamation 'Don't!', read as a verb: refrain.
explanation.definitionFit: To refrain is to not do something, which 'Don't!' commands.

clue.text: Your quiet fury, after answer divided county

indicators.note: the other pieces follow A

parts.note: A = answer
yr is an abbreviation of your
sh! is a call for quiet
ire is anger

explanation.surface: Someone's quiet rage after getting an answer that split a county.
explanation.walkthrough: Ayrshire is a county in south-west Scotland, now split into North, South and East Ayrshire, hence 'divided'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ayrshire is a Scottish county divided into three council areas.

clue.text: A useless board ousting leader is possible to prevent

indicators.note: the first letter of TABLE is removed

parts.note: kept as is
void = invalid, of no use
a table is a board; TABLE without its first letter

explanation.surface: A company's useless board of directors throws out its chairman to head off trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' suggests directors and 'leader' a chairman; here the board is a table and the leader its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an accident that could have been headed off is one that need never have happened.

clue.text: Only a little fuel in rocket for the moment

indicators.note: only a small part, the first letter, of fuel is used

parts.note: to rocket is to rise fast, to soar
first letter of fuel

explanation.surface: A rocket has barely any fuel left for now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocket' looks like a noun, but it is the verb, meaning to shoot up.
explanation.definitionFit: 'So far' means up to now, as things stand for the moment.

clue.text: Failure of more soldiers taking part in retreat

indicators.note: the answer is part of the words that follow
to retreat is to go back, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words: the end of 'more' and the start of 'soldiers'

explanation.surface: An army's defeat in which extra troops joined the withdrawal.
explanation.walkthrough: The military words all belong to the scene; the only definition is 'Failure', a person as much as an event.
explanation.definitionFit: A loser is a failure, someone who never succeeds.

clue.text: People who've paid for event fail to go without being asked to

parts.note: the gate is the paying attendance at a sports event
to crash is to fail, as a business or computer does

explanation.surface: Ticket-holders complain that a paid event fails, while others turn up uninvited.
explanation.walkthrough: The gate is British for the number of paying spectators at a match.
explanation.definitionFit: To gatecrash is to attend a party or event without an invitation.

clue.text: Speculate wildly about one minute object maybe buried in foundations

indicators.note: the letters of SPECULATE are scrambled

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters
I = one, the Roman numeral
M = minute

explanation.surface: Someone guesses wildly about a tiny object hidden under a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' reads as tiny, describing the object, but it is the abbreviation M.
explanation.definitionFit: A time capsule is a container of objects buried, often in a building's foundations, for future discovery.

clue.text: Sailor cursed clumsy American intern

indicators.note: clumsy = badly put together, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: A sailor swears at a clumsy young American on work placement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cursed' looks like the sailor swearing; it belongs to the definition, as Coleridge's mariner was cursed for shooting the albatross.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ancient Mariner is the sailor under a curse in Coleridge's poem.

clue.text: Came back bloody, holding foot with end of toe severed

parts.note: blood is red
a spondee is a metrical foot of two long syllables
last letter of toe; removed from SPONDEE

explanation.surface: Someone returns bloodied, clutching a foot with the tip of a toe cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' and 'toe' paint an injury, but the foot is a unit of verse; losing E (the end of toe) turns SPONDEE into SPONDE.
explanation.definitionFit: To respond is to reply, to come back with an answer.

clue.text: Pen catalogues for elegant writers

parts.note: a sty is a pen for pigs
a catalogue is a list

explanation.surface: Pens and catalogues offered for fine writers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' suggests writing, which fits the definition; it is the animal enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: Stylists are writers who pay special attention to elegant style.

clue.text: Formal wear matching furniture almost entirely

indicators.note: the whole phrase is used except its last letter

parts.note: a three-piece suite is a matching sofa and two armchairs; its final E is dropped

explanation.surface: An outfit so coordinated it almost matches the sofa.
explanation.walkthrough: A three-piece suite is the British term for a matching sofa and two armchairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A three-piece suit, jacket, waistcoat and trousers, is formal dress.

clue.text: Soldier's ridiculously larger uniform

indicators.note: the letters are arranged absurdly, i.e. rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters
Uniform is U in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A soldier's uniform is absurdly oversized.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', linking definition to wordplay, not a possessive. 'Uniform' looks like army kit but is just the letter U.
explanation.definitionFit: A regular is a professional soldier in a standing army.

clue.text: More irritating vessel one fills having no lid

indicators.note: I fills, i.e. goes inside, the vessel
in a down clue the lid is the top letter, so P goes

parts.note: a pitcher is a jug; PITCHER without its first letter
I = one, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A pot, filled up with its lid left off, gets more annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, the lid of a word is its first letter, sitting on top.
explanation.definitionFit: Itchier means causing more itching, so more irritating.

clue.text: Show sadness about a good couple like Cliff and Ben perhaps

parts.note: to cry is to show sadness
kept as is
G = good, twice

explanation.surface: Someone weeps over a lovely pair of men named Cliff and Ben.
explanation.walkthrough: Cliff and Ben look like first names; lower-case, a cliff is a rock face and a ben a Scottish mountain, both rugged.
explanation.definitionFit: Craggy means rugged and rocky, as a cliff or a mountain is.

clue.text: Lands in safety vessel

parts.note: a bird lights, or alights, on a branch when it lands
in = fashionable, hip

explanation.surface: A craft comes ashore inside a rescue boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link or a container signal; it is a word in its own right, meaning fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: A lightship is a moored vessel with a beacon that warns shipping of danger.

clue.text: Now sycophant gets daughter up

indicators.note: the sycophant gets, i.e. has done to it, the move
in a down clue, up means higher, so D moves above A

parts.note: a toady is a flatterer
D = daughter; it adds no letters, it names the D already in TOADY that moves

explanation.surface: A flatterer rouses a daughter out of bed this morning.
explanation.walkthrough: Not a full shuffle: only the D moves, one place up the column, turning TOADY into TODAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Today means at the present time, now.

clue.text: Award nothing, bad mark

parts.note: O looks like zero
a scar is a lasting mark from an injury

explanation.surface: A contestant wins no prize, just a black mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Award nothing' reads as a verb phrase, but 'Award' alone is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oscar is an award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

clue.text: Sulphur, foul-smelling and compact

parts.note: S is the chemical symbol for sulphur
olid is a rare word for foul-smelling

explanation.surface: A chemist describes sulphur as smelly and dense.
explanation.walkthrough: OLID is an obscure word from the Latin for 'to smell'; it turns up in crosswords more than anywhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: dense, firmly packed matter with no gaps.

clue.text: United in caressing abandoned child

indicators.note: in places one thing within another

parts.note: fondling = stroking, caressing
U = United, as in football club names

explanation.surface: Two people are united in cuddling an orphaned child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'United in' reads as a phrase meaning together; the U is the letter that goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A foundling is an infant found after being abandoned by its parents.

clue.text: Fine Irish? This could be Scotch

parts.note: F = fine, as on pencil grades
Ir. = Irish

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a fine Irish whiskey might pass for Scotch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch' suggests whisky; it is the tree, the Scotch fir, another name for the Scots pine.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Scots pine is also called the Scotch fir, so one conifer of this kind is Scotch.

clue.text: Small request for aerosol

parts.note: S = small, as on clothing sizes
a prayer is a request, especially to God

explanation.surface: A modest plea for a can of spray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Request' leads to PRAYER, an earnest plea, not to the verb ask.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a pressurised can that releases a fine mist is a device for spraying.

clue.text: Getting on TV, not at first receiving colour back

indicators.note: the first letter of TELLY is dropped
the colour is written backwards

parts.note: telly is British slang for TV; TELLY without its first letter
RED, reversed

explanation.surface: Someone getting on TV for the first time is taking on colour again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting on TV' reads as appearing on television; 'Getting on' alone is the definition, meaning ageing.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'getting on' is short for getting on in years, a polite way to say old.
